newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Key figure behind Ceausescu fall ends silence.
newsitem.headline: Key figure behind Ceausescu fall ends silence.

text.p: An army general who held key jobs in Romania's first post-communist government ended seven years of silence on Thursday and said he had persuaded dictator Nicolae Ceausescu into his doomed 1989 flight from power.

Victor Stanculescu, a former economy, defence and industry minister, said a handful of people who seized power during the bloody December 1989 revolt had decided Ceausescu's fate in a defence ministry lavatory on Christmas day.

"I persuaded him (Ceausescu) and his wife Elena to flee Bucharest by helicopter, to escape mob lynching," Stanculescu, a former army general turned businessman, told a midnight show hosted by a private television company.
Stanculescu said he put his leg in a plaster cast to escape carrying out Ceausescu's orders to have the army turn their guns on demonstrators.

Around 1,500 people were killed across Romania, most during chaotic clashes between the army and the police after Ceausescu was plucked from the roof of the Communist Party central committee building. The couple were summarily tried and shot by firing squad in a barracks northwest of Bucharest.

Stanculescu said the decision to have Ceausescu and his wife executed was taken by an inner group which swept to power during the uprising around ex-president Ion Iliescu, including former Prime Minister Petre Roman.

"It was a group decision. They went to the bathroom of the defence ministry, because they thought it was the only safe place to talk," said Stanculescu, one of the witnesses shown on a film taken at the Ceausescus' Christmas 1989 trial.
"I was not tempted to take power myself," said Stanculescu, tipped as a possible military leader for a time when ethnic and political violence shook Romania in the early 1990s.

"Romania had had enough dictatorships," he said in a reference to pre-war dictatorship under King Carol II, Marshal Ion Antonescu's World War Two regime and tough communist rulers Ceausescu and his predecessor Gheorghe Gheorghiu Dej.

Stanculescu, now 69, is local representative of a British-based group he said had a turnover of $220 million from metal trade last year. He said he had earned $10 billion for Romania during the 1980s as head of the army's procurement under Ceausescu but had since abandoned such activity.

He spoke of early disagreements with Iliescu -- ousted by reformist Emil Constantinescu in last November's elections -- over June 1990 riots in which six people were killed when pro-government miners' mobs beat up protesters in Bucharest.
"It was a stupid initiative to call in the miners," said Stanculescu, who held the three portfolios under Roman.

He had turned down an offer to take over as Prime Minister when Roman was forced to quit during a second wave of miners' unrest in 1991. "I'd have agreed, had Iliescu been meddling less in government affairs."
